By decadeCompare

The lists, in their own time

Publication years organise this archive. A title such as Megatrends 2000 names a horizon. It appeared in 1990. The entries paraphrase each work and identify its scope. Forecasts, survey rankings, demographic projections and methods reviews each answer a different question.

No matching publications. Try a broader search or another decade.

1980s

America looks past the factory

Naisbitt started with American newspapers and described changes people could already recognise in their jobs, communities and choices. His ten directions often had a destination: a society organised around information, networks and participation.

1982John NaisbittMegatrends: Ten New Directions Transforming Our Lives

American society

Naisbitt read local news for signs that Americans were changing how they worked, lived and organised. He presented ten paired shifts. Their geography matters, especially in his account of Americans moving south and west.

Compare this editionBack to this comparison
  • From factories to information work

    Creating, handling and circulating information were becoming central economic activities.

  • High tech, high touch

    As machines entered more settings, people would seek personal attention, human contact and opportunities to participate.

  • National economies become interdependent

    US firms and workers increasingly faced decisions shaped by trade, investment and production abroad.

  • Planning beyond the next quarter

    The book anticipated more attention to the longer consequences of decisions in business and public life.

  • Decisions move closer to communities

    States, towns and local initiatives would gain influence as large central institutions lost authority.

  • From institutional provision to self-help

    People would organise around shared needs and take more responsibility for their own welfare.

  • Citizens seek a direct say

    Voting for representatives would sit alongside participation in decisions affecting workplaces and communities.

  • Networks challenge hierarchies

    People could share information across organisational boundaries and coordinate through informal relationships.

  • The American Sun Belt gains weight

    Population and business shifted from the US industrial North towards southern and western states. This was a domestic shift.

  • More ways to live

    Mass markets and binary social choices gave way to a wider range of careers, products and lifestyles.

SourcesMegatrends: Ten New Directions Transforming Our Lives

1990s

The world opens up, unevenly

The 1990 book took a global view of markets, culture, faith and biology. Later books examined women’s power and Asian economies in their own right. Global lifestyles and cultural nationalism sat side by side even in this optimistic period.

1990John Naisbitt and Patricia AburdeneMegatrends 2000: Ten New Directions for the 1990s

Global business and culture

Published in 1990, the sequel widened its geographical reach. The authors connected economic integration with surprising cultural responses, including renewed attachment to national identity and religion.

Compare this editionBack to this comparison
  • A decade of worldwide economic expansion

    The authors expected a long global upswing as markets opened and commerce crossed borders.

  • An arts revival

    They expected attendance, investment and participation in the arts to expand.

  • Socialism adopts market mechanisms

    Market reforms in socialist economies suggested possible combinations of public goals and price signals.

  • Global lifestyles and cultural belonging

    Shared consumer habits could grow alongside stronger assertions of national languages and traditions.

  • Welfare provision shifts to private hands

    Governments would transfer some responsibility for public services and social protection to other providers.

  • The Pacific becomes an economic centre

    Trade and economic dynamism around the Pacific would redraw the map of opportunity.

  • Women gain leadership roles

    Women would take on greater authority in organisations, enterprise and politics.

  • Biology becomes a defining science

    Biotechnology would create business opportunities and bring choices about living systems into public debate.

  • Religion gains influence

    The approach of the millennium would stimulate spiritual searching across established and newer religious movements.

  • Individuals gain agency

    Personal initiative and choice would gain influence over institutions and collective orthodoxies.

SourcesMegatrends 2000: Ten New Directions for the 1990s
Related reading

1992Patricia Aburdene and John NaisbittMegatrends for Women

Gender and institutional power

The authors turned a single 1990 heading into a book on changing institutions. They also predicted a woman would be US president by 2004. That missed deadline illustrates the distance between identifying a direction and timing a particular event. These are themes highlighted in the publisher’s description.

Compare this editionBack to this comparison
  • Electoral representation

    The authors read growing numbers of women standing for office as a sign that the presidency could soon follow.

  • Enterprise and management

    Women building businesses and leading workplaces were changing who held economic authority and how management was practised.

  • Civic leadership

    Organising around housing, public safety and the environment gave women a route to shaping public priorities.

  • Sport and fitness

    Participation in everyday sport and success in elite competition challenged assumptions about who belonged in athletics.

  • Health and medical research

    Women’s advocacy around ageing, heart disease and breast cancer could reshape clinical and research priorities.

  • Religious authority

    Women leaders and theologians questioned inherited accounts of spiritual authority and divinity.

  • Fashion and cultural production

    Women designers assumed authority in an industry whose senior creative roles often went to men.

  • Politics after the Cold War

    The authors thought domestic issues would command more attention, opening new opportunities for women in public leadership.

SourcesMegatrends for Women
1996John NaisbittMegatrends Asia

Asian economies and societies

Naisbitt asked how growth driven within Asia might change the global economy. He put business networks with links to Chinese diaspora communities at the centre of his account. His eight shifts generalised across very different countries.

Compare this editionBack to this comparison
  • Business networks cross national borders

    Family, commercial and diaspora relationships linked economic activity across several jurisdictions.

  • Domestic consumers drive demand

    Household spending within Asian markets would become a stronger engine of growth alongside exports.

  • Modernisation on Asian terms

    Prosperity could strengthen local cultural identities and development models.

  • Markets gain influence over investment

    The author expected private enterprise to gain scope in economies shaped by government direction.

  • Growth concentrates in large cities

    Migration and investment would transform previously rural societies and enlarge metropolitan centres.

  • Industry moves into advanced technology

    Manufacturers could move beyond labour-intensive production into higher-value goods and capabilities.

  • Women gain economic influence

    Changing employment and business opportunities would challenge male control of leadership positions.

  • The world’s economic centre shifts east

    Asian economies together would reshape patterns of global opportunity and influence.

SourcesMegatrends Asia
2000s

Globalisation acquires a politics

A business author asked whether values could reshape capitalism. Security analysts asked who gained from integration and who could disrupt it. Between its 2004 and 2008 outlooks, the US National Intelligence Council gave greater weight to a world with several centres of power.

2004US National Intelligence CouncilMapping the Global Future

Global security outlook to 2020

The Council consulted experts internationally and explored four alternative futures. It treated globalisation as a force shaping the other developments, while asking who would benefit and where it might provoke resistance. The entries below are its four principal analytical themes.

Compare this editionBack to this comparison
  • The uneven gains of globalisation

    Faster flows of capital, labour and technology could create wealth while unsettling jobs and intensifying domestic political tensions.

  • New powers, especially China and India

    The relative rise of large Asian economies could change alliances, energy demand and the position of the United States.

  • Governance struggles to keep pace

    Democratic change, identity politics and international institutions’ ability to manage cross-border problems could diverge.

  • Persistent insecurity

    Conflict, terrorism and fear could remain politically potent even if many people became more prosperous.

SourcesMapping the Global Future
2005Patricia AburdeneMegatrends 2010: The Rise of Conscious Capitalism

US business and values

Aburdene brought the 1990 themes of individual agency and spiritual revival into the workplace. Her seven substantive chapters asked whether managers, consumers and investors could change the purposes companies serve.

Compare this editionBack to this comparison
  • Personal spirituality influences organisations

    The search for meaning in individuals’ working lives could shape the cultures of entire organisations.

  • Business takes wider responsibilities

    Companies would increasingly consider employees, communities and environmental impacts when defining success.

  • Middle managers lead change

    People with limited formal authority could shift company behaviour through everyday management decisions.

  • Faith and reflection enter working life

    Employees and managers were making space for spiritual practices and discussion at work.

  • Purchases express values

    Some customers would choose goods according to a producer’s social and environmental conduct.

  • Conscious practices become management tools

    The book considered ways firms could apply reflective practices to workplace problems and examine the results.

  • Investment incorporates social criteria

    Investors could direct capital towards firms that met ethical or environmental standards.

SourcesMegatrends 2010: The Rise of Conscious Capitalism
2008US National Intelligence CouncilGlobal Trends 2025: A Transformed World

Global security outlook to 2025

The Council moved multipolarity closer to the centre of its outlook and explored four alternative futures. Its seven analytical chapters already put demographic divergence, resource insecurity and the politics of interdependence on the agenda.

Compare this editionBack to this comparison
  • The world economy gains new centres

    Growth in Asia, a larger middle class and state-led capitalist models could change where wealth accumulated and who set the rules.

  • Age structures pull countries apart

    Some populations would shrink and age while others retained large younger cohorts. Migration and urbanisation could change the consequences.

  • More states gain international influence

    China, India and other rising powers would have greater capacity to shape regional and global decisions.

  • Resources grow more contested

    Energy transitions, demand for water and food, and climate stress could shift the balance between importers and exporters.

  • New pressures for conflict

    Resource competition, instability and the spread of military capabilities could strain relations within and between states.

  • Global institutions face harder problems

    More centres of power could make cooperation harder even as transnational networks gained influence.

  • US leadership requires power sharing

    A still powerful United States could face tighter constraints and greater reliance on partners.

SourcesGlobal Trends 2025: A Transformed World

2010s

A policy vocabulary takes shape

Ageing, urban growth, technological change, resources and shifting economic power recur. The institutional lens now matters enormously. A public-finance team sees debt, a science agency sees biodiversity, and a European policy lab sees migration, learning and governance.

2012CSIRO FuturesOur Future World

Australian science foresight

Australia’s national science agency revised its 2010 draft after feedback from researchers, businesses and communities. Looking towards 2032 from Australia changes the geography of the story. Rising incomes in Asia mean new tourists, investors and intellectual exchange as well as new markets.

Compare this editionBack to this comparison
  • More from less

    Growing demand puts pressure on water, food, energy and minerals. Efficiency and changes in consumption could stretch supplies.

  • Going, going … gone?

    Habitat and species loss can become permanent. The question mark leaves room for conservation to alter the outcome.

  • The silk highway

    Asian growth redirects trade, capital, tourism and ideas, reshaping Australia’s relationships with its neighbours.

  • Forever young

    Older populations bring accumulated skills and experience as well as new demands on care, pensions and employment.

  • Virtually here

    Shopping, public services, work and relationships increasingly take place online.

  • Great expectations

    Consumers seek personalised services and memorable experiences. Relationships can matter more than acquiring another possession.

SourcesOur Future World
Related reading

  • Climate & place
  • Health & care
2013KPMG International and the Mowat CentreFuture State 2030

Government strategy

The 2013 study asked what nine global changes would mean for national governments. Public borrowing earns a place alongside climate and demography because a government’s ability to finance services shapes how citizens experience those changes.

Compare this editionBack to this comparison
  • Population structure

    Some governments face pension and care pressures while others must create jobs for large younger cohorts.

  • Individual empowerment

    Better education, health and communications raise expectations of participation and transparency.

  • Technology as an enabler

    New tools expand what governments can deliver while creating difficult regulatory choices.

  • Economic interdependence

    Cross-border trade and investment spread both economic gains and financial shocks.

  • Public debt

    Servicing debt can squeeze the resources available for future public services.

  • Shifting economic power

    Emerging economies gain bargaining power over the rules of trade and investment.

  • Climate change

    Governments face decisions about cutting emissions, adapting infrastructure and sharing the costs.

  • Strains on resources

    Demand for water, energy and food puts competing users into closer contact.

  • Urban growth

    Fast-growing cities must fund housing, transport and services at the pace of settlement.

SourcesFuture State 2030
Related reading
  • Trade & economies
  • Participation & politics
2014PwCFive Global Megatrends

Business outlook

Five members of PwC’s network leadership each picked a force likely to matter to clients over the following decade. The short list offered businesses a shared vocabulary. Demographic divergence was already explicit in its first item.

Compare this editionBack to this comparison
  • Population shifts

    Workforces and demand for services diverge between countries with rapid ageing and countries with youthful growth.

  • Economic power moves

    Emerging economies gain weight as markets and sources of investment.

  • Faster urbanisation

    More economic activity concentrates in cities, increasing demand for infrastructure.

  • Climate and resource pressures

    Growing demand for food, water and energy coincides with climatic disruption.

  • Technological breakthroughs

    Digital tools alter products, business models and the speed of competition.

SourcesFive Global Megatrends
2016OECDScience, Technology and Innovation Outlook 2016

Innovation policy

Chapter one groups the forces bearing on research and innovation into eight themes, with a typical horizon of 10–15 years. The relationship works in both directions. Ageing can steer research towards care technologies, while new treatments can change what an ageing population needs.

Compare this editionBack to this comparison
  • Population change

    Ageing, growth and migration reshape the supply of skills and the needs research addresses.

  • Energy and natural resources

    Food, water and energy pressures make efficiency and alternative supplies research priorities.

  • Climate and ecosystems

    Environmental damage creates demand for cleaner technologies and adaptation.

  • Global integration

    Knowledge, investment and research cross borders. Countries can collaborate while competing for their benefits.

  • Government’s evolving role

    Public funding, regulation and international cooperation help determine which innovations reach people.

  • Employment and productivity

    Changes in growth, skills and automation raise questions about jobs and how productivity gains are shared.

  • Social change

    Urban growth, education and shifting expectations alter who participates in innovation.

  • Health and unequal well-being

    Disease burdens and unequal access influence medical priorities and who benefits from advances.

SourcesScience, Technology and Innovation Outlook 2016
2018European Commission Joint Research CentreMegatrends Hub

European public policy

Development began in 2016 and the public Hub opened in 2018. Its fourteen forces are global, selected for their relevance to Europe. The launch booklet emphasised the changing forms of inequality and the spread of consumerism. Later Hub entries also emphasise widening inequalities and growing consumption.

Compare this editionBack to this comparison
  • More connected technologies

    Digital networks connect work, government, production and social life.

  • Pressure on resources

    Demand intensifies competition for land, water, energy and materials.

  • Changing work

    Automation and new business models alter occupations and working conditions.

  • New security threats

    Threats arise from a wider range of actors and extend across borders.

  • Climate and ecosystem damage

    Warming, pollution and biodiversity loss change the conditions societies depend on.

  • Continuing urbanisation

    Cities gain people and influence, widening demands on services.

  • More ways to learn

    Learning stretches across a lifetime, through more providers and channels.

  • Changing inequalities

    Disadvantage takes different forms across places, generations and social groups.

  • Influence moves east and south

    Emerging economies gain influence over global affairs.

  • Growing consumer culture

    Rising purchasing power changes demand and environmental footprints.

  • Diverging populations

    Growth, ageing and shrinking populations coexist across regions.

  • New forms of governance

    Cities, networks and other actors share influence with national authorities.

  • Migration’s growing significance

    Cross-border movement becomes more consequential for economies and politics.

  • Changing health burdens

    Lifestyle, ageing and environmental exposures reshape health needs.

SourcesMegatrends Hub

2020s

Living with the consequences

Reports foreground adaptation, rivalry, the reliability of information and the authority delegated to machines. The remit still shapes the list. A humanitarian or development lens foregrounds distribution, while an investment outlook distinguishes technologies that attract capital.

2020Filippo Artuso and Irene Guijt, OxfamGlobal Megatrends: Mapping the Forces that Affect Us All

International development

The authors compared 22 scans and organised their findings into four clusters. For organisations tackling poverty, they asked whose experience broad labels conceal. Gender, civic freedoms and the causes of conflict received too little attention in the underlying literature.

Compare this editionBack to this comparison
  • Technological innovation

    Automation can improve services and concentrate gains among technology owners.

  • Hyperconnectivity

    Networks speed communication, commerce and surveillance.

  • Changing work

    Platform work can increase flexibility and expose workers to insecurity.

  • Age structures

    Youthful populations need employment opportunities. Older populations change care needs.

  • Urbanisation

    Fast-growing settlements may outpace water, housing and transport provision.

  • Migration

    Movement creates opportunities while exposing some migrants to exploitation.

  • Health challenges

    New treatments, mobility and population ageing reshape disease burdens.

  • Climate change

    Heat, flooding and disrupted livelihoods affect groups with different means to adapt.

  • Resource scarcity

    Unequal access to water, food and energy compounds hardship.

  • Multipolarity

    New centres of economic and political influence contest existing rules.

  • Economic inequality

    Gaps in income and wealth persist within and across countries.

  • Conflict

    Interacting political and resource pressures can increase insecurity.

  • Weakening social cohesion

    Polarisation and institutional distrust make collective decisions harder.

SourcesGlobal Megatrends: Mapping the Forces that Affect Us All
2020United Nations Economist NetworkShaping the Trends of Our Time

Sustainable development

Five forces form a test of progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals. The UN economists ask how policy can change their direction and who shares in their benefits.

Compare this editionBack to this comparison

  • Urbanisation

  • Digital technologies

2024Claire Naughtin, Emma Schleiger, Alexandra Bratanova, Andrew Terhorst and Stefan HajkowiczForty Years in the Making

Systematic review of methods

This review examined 267 academic and practitioner publications from 1982–2022. It found considerable variation in definitions and methods. Its contribution is a way to test a candidate’s breadth, duration, influence across domains and relevance to future change, and a process for developing and validating claims. A repeated label across reports may trace back to a common source.

Compare this editionBack to this comparison

This review describes how researchers identify megatrends.

SourcesForty Years in the Making
2024UN DESA Population DivisionWorld Population Prospects 2024

Demographic estimates and projections

An empirical check on demographic divergence. The UN groups 237 countries and areas by the timing of their population peak. The future groups describe projections subject to assumptions about fertility, mortality and migration.

Compare this editionBack to this comparison
  • Already past peak population

    By 2024, the population had already peaked in 63 countries and areas, including China, Germany and Japan.

  • Projected to peak within three decades

    The UN projects a peak between 2025 and 2054 for 48 countries and areas, including Brazil, Iran and Viet Nam.

  • Projected to grow through 2054

    The other 126, including India, Nigeria and the United States, are expected to keep growing through 2054. The contribution of migration varies.

SourcesWorld Population Prospects 2024

Expert risk perceptions

The survey measures expected severity. Four underlying structural forces, first identified in the 2024 edition, help explain why respondents rank risks differently over two and ten years. The two lists below are in rank order.

    New capabilities spread opportunities and vulnerabilities across systems.

  • Changing geopolitical power

    Rivalries and contested alliances alter who sets the rules.

  • A changing climate

  • Diverging populations

    Differences in population growth and age structure widen.

  • Two-year risk ranking

    1 economic confrontation, 2 false information, 3 polarisation, 4 extreme weather, 5 armed conflict involving states, 6 digital insecurity, 7 inequality, 8 loss of rights and civic freedoms, 9 pollution, 10 forced movement.

  • Ten-year risk ranking

    1 extreme weather, 2 biodiversity and ecosystem loss, 3 major Earth-system changes, 4 false information, 5 AI harms, 6 resource shortages, 7 inequality, 8 digital insecurity, 9 polarisation, 10 pollution.
